Day 1.

Purchase a USDA Prime rib roast. I prefer bone in, but Bob from the meat department at the grocery store failed me. He said he would get me a 4 bone thick rib roast, bone in, as long as I call in and left him a good review. Fuck you, Bob, you didn't get my God damned rib roast, you get no review from me. Or, better yet, I'll call in and give you a shit review. Lying sack of shit.

Anyway, what you do in order to dry age at home is get a roasting pan like pictured. I don't know if salt makes a difference, but I throw some on the bottom of the pan.

Then, wrap it up in a cheese cloth. I've read that paper towels work too.

Put it in the fridge. For the first three days, pull it out, unwrap it, and rewrap it, so the cloth or paper towels don't glue themselves to it.

Just let it sit for a month or so. Longest I've done is 35 days. This time I'm going for 40 days.

After that, I'll pull it out and cut the hard outer shell off. I'll lose about a whole steak worth of meat from the process, but it's worth it. After I'm done shaving it down, I'll cut it into 3-4 ribeye steaks. 3-4 depending on how thick I cut them.

Why do this? The flavor. All the enzymes and shit work their way inside the roast as the water evaporates from the outside. It also makes it more tender.

Grill them up, and I'll have some Grade A steakhouse steaks that I didn't even have to dress up for.

Edit: Also, bone-in is better because it's less meat you have to shave away. The side where the bone is on is protected by the bone, so you don't have to shave it off. And the meat near the bone cooks less on the inside, so the best bites are closest to the bone.
Ok, so...how on earth does it not spoil? That darkened spot on the outside edge looks pretty gnarly.

Good question!

Magic!

The magical layer surrounding the meet protects it from rotting!

Honestly, I don't know. The cold keeps microbes from spreading while the meat dries out. It's magic.

Just cut it off, no worries. As long as you keep it dry on the outside it will not rot. Kenji at the food lab does good work.

OP-Nice work. How was the smell?

Smell is awesome. Every time I open my fridge I get blasted with this meaty, somewhat buttery - but not really, aroma that makes me want to just take a bite out of it.

From what I've read, the dried out parts aren't spoiled, and you can actually eat it or cook it. I haven't tried this, it's harder than beef jerky. I usually feed it to my dogs, and they're fine.

It spoils because of bad bacteria. Bad bacteria need water and food. The cheesecloth/paper towel step dries out the outer layer, so there's no water for the bacteria. The inner stuff is inner, so the bacteria can't get in there if you don't cut it up.

The dried skin creates a barrier that bacteria can't live on, and can't get through. The enzymes inside that do the work are good, and they are already in the cow when you put a spike through its brain.
There's nothing better than a dry aged ribeye. It really concentrates the beef flavor and develops a kind of nutty/earthy flavor that is just great.
